## From Context Tokens to KV State {#sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry}

When an inference service executes an autoregressive language model, the physical memory of the accelerator is rapidly dominated not by the static parameters of the neural network, but by the dynamic activation state accumulated across active request trajectories. In traditional stateless request-reply systems, this state was transient and negligible; a user submitted a short prompt, the model generated a paragraph, and the runtime immediately reclaimed the intermediate tensors. Autonomous agents destroy this operational simplicity. As an agent inspects files, runs build scripts, parses compiler diagnostics, and iterates across multi-step execution plans, the sequence length expands from hundreds of tokens to tens or hundreds of thousands. At these sequence lengths, the physical attention state—retained across forward passes to prevent catastrophic recomputation—swells to tens of gigabytes per active trajectory. If the serving runtime treats this state as an opaque, contiguous buffer, accelerator memory exhausts within a handful of concurrent requests, triggering out-of-memory faults and stalling the host supervisor.

::: {.column-margin}
![Tensor geometry of key and value projections stored in accelerator high-bandwidth memory across transformer layers.](images/svg/prompt_context_window_anatomy.svg){#fig-vol3-kv-geometry}
:::

**The key-value cache is the retained physical attention state of a transformer sequence; its byte footprint is dictated strictly by model geometry and active token count, establishing the fundamental concurrency ceiling of the serving runtime.** Understanding the physical mechanics of this cache is the prerequisite for designing agent serving systems. Where Chapter 04 addressed the logical selection and compaction of context tokens in the host agent runtime, this chapter examines the concrete, physical memory allocations inside the neural accelerator. A serving runtime cannot virtualize or schedule what it cannot measure. To build dependable agent runtimes, systems engineers must derive the exact memory footprint of attention tensors, characterize how model architectural variants alter state volume, and analyze the physical trade-off between retaining activations in high-bandwidth memory and recomputing them on demand.

The inflection point from conversational chatbots to autonomous agents fundamentally alters the lifecycle of inference memory. A conversational interface is typically synchronous, short-lived, and monotonic: each turn appends a brief user query, generates a bounded response, and terminates. In contrast, an agentic system delegates high-order engineering workflows to an unprivileged foundation model that operates in a closed loop with an external environment. The context contains deep directory hierarchies, abstracted symbol graphs, dense execution logs, and historical tool invocations. Because the generation of each new token requires attending over every preceding token in the trajectory, the model cannot simply discard its past. Every observation returned by a bash tool or language server must be projected into the model's internal vector space and retained for future attention operations. What was once an ephemeral working scratchpad becomes a long-lived, high-occupancy memory structure that persists across dozens of discrete tool-execution cycles.

::: {.column-margin}
**Attention Head Topologies:**
In Multi-Head Attention (MHA), $H_{\text{kv}} = H_{\text{q}}$, maintaining separate key and value heads for every query head. In Multi-Query Attention (MQA), $H_{\text{kv}} = 1$, collapsing all key and value projections into a single shared head. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) groups query heads into $H_{\text{kv}} = H_{\text{q}} / G$ clusters, providing an intermediate design that dramatically curbs KV memory while preserving modeling expressiveness.
:::

To understand why this memory footprint accumulates, we must confront the physical boundary of the foundation model itself. Operating under zero ambient authority ($A=0$), the foundation model is an unprivileged statistical predictor executing purely functional forward tensor operations; it possesses no persistent internal registers, no ambient storage, and no autonomous background threads. Autoregressive token generation proceeds in discrete, sequential steps. At generation step $t$, the host runtime feeds the newly predicted token $x_t$ into the network. Within each transformer layer, this token's hidden state vector is mapped through three learned linear projections to yield a query vector $q_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{head}}}$, a key vector $k_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{head}}}$, and a value vector $v_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{head}}}$ for each attention head. The scaled dot-product attention mechanism computes an output representation by evaluating:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}}\right)V$$

For the newly arriving token at position $t$, its query vector $q_t$ must compute an inner product against the key vectors of *all* prior positions $i \in \{1, \dots, t\}$ to produce the attention distribution, which is subsequently used to compute a weighted sum over all corresponding value vectors $v_i$. Herein lies the central systems confrontation: although the prior tokens $x_1, \dots, x_{t-1}$ do not change, their key and value representations are strictly required to evaluate the attention distribution at step $t$. If the serving system does not persist these intermediate $k_i$ and $v_i$ vectors, generating token $t$ requires passing the entire prefix of $t$ tokens through the network from scratch. Across a generation sequence of length $S$, this recomputation strategy incurs an aggregate computational cost scaling quadratically as $\mathcal{O}(S^2)$ in forward-pass tensor operations.

To eliminate this redundant computational overhead, inference runtimes allocate a physical buffer in accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) known as the *Key-Value (KV) cache*. During the initial context ingestion—the prefill phase—the runtime computes and stores the key and value projections for all prompt tokens. During subsequent autoregressive decoding steps, the runtime computes $q_t$, $k_t$, and $v_t$ solely for the single newly generated token, appends $k_t$ and $v_t$ to the persistent physical cache, and reads all historical keys and values from HBM to evaluate the attention equation. This optimization converts the per-token computational complexity of attention from $\mathcal{O}(t)$ back to an efficient matrix-vector evaluation. However, the runtime does not eliminate the physical cost; it merely shifts the burden from computational arithmetic to memory capacity.

The memory footprint of this retained attention state is governed strictly by the structural geometry of the underlying model and the numerical precision of the stored floating-point tensors. For a transformer model with $L$ layers, $H_{\text{kv}}$ key-value heads per layer, an attention head dimension of $d_{\text{head}}$, and a tensor storage precision of $P$ bytes per element, each individual token requires an immutable quantum of physical cache memory across the network:

$$\text{Mem}_{\text{token}} = 2 \cdot L \cdot H_{\text{kv}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot P \quad \left(\frac{\text{bytes}}{\text{token}}\right)$$

The factor of 2 accounts for the two distinct tensor projections: the key tensor and the value tensor. For a single active sequence spanning an accumulated context length of $S$ tokens, the physical memory consumed by its KV cache is:

$$\text{Mem}_{\text{seq}} = S \cdot \text{Mem}_{\text{token}} = 2 \cdot S \cdot L \cdot H_{\text{kv}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot P$$

When an inference service hosts a concurrent batch of $B$ independent agent trajectories, each operating at an average context length of $S$, the aggregate accelerator memory allocated exclusively to attention state scales linearly across all dimensions:

$$\text{Mem}_{\text{batch}} = B \cdot S \cdot \text{Mem}_{\text{token}}$$

The structural evolution of transformer architectures from Multi-Head Attention (MHA) to Multi-Query Attention (MQA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) directly reflects this physical memory wall. In classical Multi-Head Attention, the number of key-value heads equals the number of query heads ($H_{\text{kv}} = H_{\text{q}}$), meaning that an 8,192-dimensional hidden state projected across 64 heads allocates 64 distinct key heads and 64 value heads at every layer. Under MHA, the KV cache footprint quickly eclipses the static weight memory of the model itself. To alleviate this bottleneck, modern frontier architectures implement Grouped-Query Attention, wherein multiple query heads share a single key-value head group ($H_{\text{kv}} = H_{\text{q}} / G$, where $G$ is the group size). By reducing $H_{\text{kv}}$ by a factor of $G$ (typically 4 or 8), GQA compresses the physical cache footprint per token by the exact same ratio, enabling the host runtime to pack substantially more concurrent agent trajectories into physical HBM without sacrificing the modeling expressiveness provided by independent query heads.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example: Sizing the Attention State for a 70-Billion Parameter Model"}
Consider an inference cluster serving an open-weights 70-billion parameter model structured with the following architectural parameters:
- Layers ($L$): 80
- Query heads ($H_{\text{q}}$): 64
- Key-Value heads ($H_{\text{kv}}$): 8 (Grouped-Query Attention with group size $G = 8$)
- Head dimension ($d_{\text{head}}$): 128
- Storage precision ($P$): 2 bytes (16-bit brain floating-point, `bfloat16`)

Using the physical derivation:
$$\text{Mem}_{\text{token}} = 2 \cdot 80 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 327,680 \text{ bytes/token} = 320 \text{ KiB/token}$$

Now evaluate the physical memory footprint across three realistic agent context regimes:
1. **Standard Turn ($S = 8,192$ tokens):**
   $$\text{Mem}_{\text{seq}} = 8,192 \cdot 327,680 \text{ B} = 2,684,354,560 \text{ B} \approx 2.50 \text{ GiB}$$
2. **Deep Diagnostic Trajectory ($S = 32,768$ tokens):**
   $$\text{Mem}_{\text{seq}} = 32,768 \cdot 327,680 \text{ B} = 10,737,418,240 \text{ B} \approx 10.00 \text{ GiB}$$
3. **Repository-Scale Context ($S = 131,072$ tokens):**
   $$\text{Mem}_{\text{seq}} = 131,072 \cdot 327,680 \text{ B} = 42,949,672,960 \text{ B} \approx 40.00 \text{ GiB}$$

Had this model been designed using Multi-Head Attention ($H_{\text{kv}} = 64$), the memory consumption would scale eightfold: a single 131,072-token sequence would demand $320.00 \text{ GiB}$ of physical memory purely for its key-value projections—an allocation that exceeds the entire onboard memory capacity of four 80 GiB NVIDIA H100 GPUs combined.
:::

This quantitative reality establishes a rigid capacity boundary on the inference serving system. Consider an enterprise inference node provisioned with 8 discrete accelerators, each possessing 80 GiB of high-bandwidth memory, providing an aggregate pool of $\text{HBM}_{\text{total}} = 640 \text{ GiB}$. The 70-billion parameter model, loaded in 16-bit precision, consumes roughly $\text{Mem}_{\text{weights}} \approx 140 \text{ GiB}$ of memory across the cluster. Reserving an additional $\text{Mem}_{\text{runtime}} \approx 20 \text{ GiB}$ for communication buffers, NCCL scratch spaces, and activation workspaces during the prefill forward pass leaves approximately $\text{Mem}_{\text{kv\_available}} = 480 \text{ GiB}$ dedicated to the dynamic attention cache. The maximum theoretical concurrency ceiling $B_{\max}$ of active agent trajectories running concurrently at context length $S$ is strictly governed by the floor quotient:

$$B_{\max} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{HBM}_{\text{total}} - \text{Mem}_{\text{weights}} - \text{Mem}_{\text{runtime}}}{\text{Mem}_{\text{seq}}} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{480 \text{ GiB}}{S \cdot 320 \text{ KiB}} \right\rfloor$$

When agent sequences are short ($S = 8,192$), the cluster comfortably hosts $B_{\max} = \lfloor 480 / 2.5 \rfloor = 192$ concurrent trajectories. But as soon as those agents ingest complex codebases and run multi-step execution traces that drive context to $S = 131,072$, the cluster's concurrency collapses to $B_{\max} = \lfloor 480 / 40 \rfloor = 12$ active trajectories. A thirteenth concurrent request cannot be scheduled; it triggers immediate queueing or causes the serving engine to fault with an accelerator out-of-memory termination.

This physical bottleneck becomes dramatically more severe when viewed through the operational lifecycle of an autonomous agent. In classical batch serving, the engine maintains continuous saturation: tokens arrive, decode loops execute uninterrupted, and the cache is deallocated the instant the final end-of-sequence token is emitted. Agentic workflows break this continuous execution assumption. An agent trajectory is an alternating sequence of neural generation phases and deterministic host tool executions. When an agent emits a tool call—such as executing a complex unit test suite or querying an external database—the generation loop halts. The neural network cannot generate the next token until the host operating system executes the command, collects standard output and standard error, and returns the observation text.

During this external execution window, the agent's physical attention state sits entirely idle inside accelerator HBM. The host runtime is confronted with a profound systems dilemma: should it retain those tens of gigabytes of KV tensors in scarce accelerator memory while waiting for the tool to return, effectively denying scheduling slots to other active requests? Or should it evict the tensors to host DRAM or discard them entirely, forcing a computationally expensive prefill recomputation phase once the tool output arrives? The foundation model cannot resolve this dilemma. Following Dijkstra's principle of external verification and Saltzer's end-to-end systems doctrine, the unprivileged model is merely an execution target; the responsibility for managing, virtualizing, and preserving physical memory across tool boundaries falls entirely upon the host serving supervisor.

If every agent trajectory possessed an invariant, statically predictable sequence length, sizing and partitioning this memory would reduce to a trivial static allocation problem. A runtime could partition its 480 GiB of available HBM into twelve fixed 40 GiB contiguous buffers, assigning one buffer to each execution slot. In production environments, however, agent trajectories are radically non-deterministic: one trajectory may succeed and terminate in 1,200 tokens, another may encounter a compiler syntax error and iterate for 45,000 tokens, and a third may spin into a recursive loop consuming the entire 131,072-token window. When an engine pre-allocates contiguous physical memory buffers based on worst-case context lengths, the overwhelming majority of allocated accelerator memory sits completely unwritten and idle, while incoming requests are rejected due to perceived capacity exhaustion. How, then, does this dynamic variation in trajectory length induce catastrophic physical memory fragmentation in contiguous allocators, and what architectural mechanisms must a serving system introduce to eliminate the resulting waste?
